newsitem.title: USA: Outlook seen dim for campaign reform.
newsitem.headline: Outlook seen dim for campaign reform.

text.p: Despite talk of unusual bipartisanship in many areas, leading congressional advocates of campaign finance reform Wednesday saw little chance of its enactment without a public outcry.
"Indeed, it (campaign reform) is stalled out in Congress," said Arizona Republican Sen. John McCain, co-sponsor with Wisconsin Democratic Sen. Russell Feingold of a new bill.

McCain, Feingold and another Senate co-sponsor, Sen. Paul Wellstone, a Minnesota Democrat, and House sponsor Martin Meehan, a Massachusetts Democrat, told a news conference there must be demands from the public before there are major changes this year in the Republican-controlled Congress.

All said it would in effect take a show of public outrage before campaign finance reform could pass Congress because incumbents who benefit from the present system and get large amounts of money fear reform.

On a separate front, the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, the lead Senate committee that will investigate reports of widespread campaign finance abuses including foreign money going to Democrats in 1996, geared up to issue subpoenas for documents for its probe.

Senate sources said "over 40" subpoenas have been prepared and "are undergoing review even as we speak." The subpoenas were being prepared even before the committee received Senate approval for $6.5 million for its investigation, an amount that is being fought by minority Democratic members.

McCain, Feingold, Wellstone and Meehan spoke at a news conference with with Common Cause President Ann McBride and New York financier Jerome Kohlberg to kick off a nationwide petition drive to collect 1,776,000 signatures demanding campaign finance reform before July 4.
President Clinton, who has endorsed the McCain-Feingold bill, also gave a boost to the petition drive, urging people to sign up to "break the logjam" holding up the legislation.

"Passage of effective campaign finance reform must be a priority for this Congress but we will succeed only if citizens all across the country make clear to elected officials that change is urgent and that public support is broad and deep," Clinton said in a statement.
While Clinton put his prestige behind the drive, he failed to win a spot for campaign finance on the congressional agenda in a meeting with congressional leaders Tuesday .
"Campaign finance reform was just mentioned very briefly," Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott said. "We have some fundamental disagreements there. So we didn't spend a lot of time there."

Besides McCain, only one other Republican has signed on to the McCain-Feingold reform bill, Senate Governmental Affairs Chairman Fred Thompson of Tennessee, who will lead the Senate probe into campaign finance abuses.

Although campaign finance reform was omitted, there was an unusual bipartisan agreement in Tuesday's meeting to press for legislative issues, including taxes, juvenile crime, education, incentives for businesses to hire those on welfare and assistance to Washington, D.C.

The McCain-Feingold measure would set voluntary spending limits by congressional candidates in return for free television time and ban big contributions to political parties among other changes designed to clean up abuses.
